title: Explain why stateful operations (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) are more expensive in parallel streams.
shortTitle: Explain why stateful operations (sorted, distinct, limit) are more expensive in parallel streams

s1_definition.profdef: Stateful intermediate operations like `sorted`, `distinct`, and `limit` need to see elements across the whole stream, so in parallel they require buffering, cross-thread coordination, and often a merge or re-sort step, which erodes the parallel benefit.
s1_definition.analogy: Sorting the whole ledger needs every page before it can finish, so splitting the work among clerks does not help much — someone still has to combine and re-order all the pages at the end.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stateful ops (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) need global knowledge, so parallel adds buffering and merge cost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Stateful intermediate operations like `sorted`, `distinct`, and `limit` need to see elements across the whole stream, so in parallel they require buffering, cross-thread coordination, and often a merge or re-sort step, which erodes the parallel benefit.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Sorting the whole ledger needs every page before it can finish, so splitting the work among clerks does not help much — someone still has to combine and re-order all the pages at the end.

**One line to remember:** Stateful ops (`sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) need global knowledge, so parallel adds buffering and merge cost.

sections.s2_technical:
Stateless operations like `filter` and `map` process each element independently, so they parallelise cleanly. Stateful operations are different: `sorted` must compare elements across all chunks, so each thread sorts its part and the framework merges them; `distinct` must track seen elements globally, requiring a shared or merged set; `limit` on an ordered parallel stream must respect encounter order, forcing coordination to pick the correct first n.

These require buffering intermediate results and extra coordination between threads, which adds memory and synchronization cost. The parallel version may be no faster or even slower than sequential for these operations, especially `limit` and `distinct` on ordered streams.

The senior nuance is matching operations to execution mode: parallel streams shine for stateless, associative, splittable work like filter-map-reduce, and are a poor fit for heavily stateful pipelines. For an ordered parallel stream, `distinct` and `limit` are particularly costly because they must preserve order; making the stream unordered with `unordered()` can relax that and speed them up when order does not matter. Recognising stateful operations as the parallel bottleneck is the key insight.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A team at the National Bank of India parallelised a pipeline that sorts and dedupes transactions and saw no speed-up, needing to understand why.

This is exactly what the stateful-operation cost explains — sorted and distinct force buffering and merging that negate parallelism.

The code contrasts a stateless parallel reduce with a stateful parallel sort in a `PipelineService.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: one million integers.

Step 1: The stateless pipeline filters and sums; each thread handles its chunk independently and the partial sums merge cheaply, so parallel helps.

Step 2: The stateful pipeline calls distinct, which must track every value seen across all chunks, needing a merged global view.

Step 3: It then calls sorted, so each thread sorts its part and the framework must merge the sorted runs into one order.

Step 4: The buffering and cross-thread coordination for distinct and sorted add cost, so the parallel version gains little or nothing over sequential.

```
INFO: stateless parallel sum : 249999500000
INFO: stateful parallel sorted-distinct size: 1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  stateless: split → [filter,map per chunk] → cheap merge(sum) → FAST parallel
  stateful:  split → distinct(global set) + sorted(sort chunks → MERGE) → costly
     stateful ops need GLOBAL view → buffering + coordination
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Stateless vs Stateful in Parallel ═══

  stateless (filter/map/reduce) → parallel wins
  stateful  (sorted/distinct/limit) → buffering+merge → little/no win
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — why stateful ops cost more in parallel ═══

  ┌─ global state requirement ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ stateless (filter/map): per-element → parallelises cleanly  │
  │ sorted: sort chunks + MERGE across threads                 │
  │ distinct: track seen GLOBALLY → shared/merged set           │
  │ limit (ordered): coordinate to pick correct first n         │
  │ → buffering + cross-thread coordination = overhead          │
  │ unordered() can relax distinct/limit order cost             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           PipelineService     │
  │  + statelessSum(List): long     │ filter+reduce (parallel-friendly)
  │  + statefulSortedDistinct(List)  │ distinct+sorted (costly parallel)
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  stateless: parallelStream.filter.mapToLong.sum
  stateful:  parallelStream.distinct.sorted.count
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Stateful intermediate operations are more expensive in parallel because they need a view of elements across the whole stream, which fights the divide-and-conquer model. Stateless operations like filter and map process each element independently, so they split cleanly across threads. But sorted must compare elements across all chunks, so each thread sorts its part and the framework has to merge the sorted runs; distinct must know every value seen globally, requiring a shared or merged set; and limit on an ordered parallel stream must coordinate threads to pick the correct first n in encounter order.

All of that means buffering intermediate results and coordinating between threads, which adds memory and synchronization cost, so the parallel version of a heavily stateful pipeline may be no faster, or even slower, than sequential. At the National Bank of India a team parallelised a sort-and-dedupe pipeline and saw no speed-up for exactly this reason.

The senior point I stress is matching operations to the execution mode: parallel streams shine for stateless, associative, splittable work like filter-map-reduce, and are a poor fit for stateful pipelines. When order does not matter I can call unordered to relax the ordering constraint on distinct and limit, which can speed them up. Recognising the stateful operations as the parallel bottleneck is what lets me decide whether to parallelise at all.

keyPoints: parallelStream() or stream().parallel() for multi-core processing
Not always faster — overhead for small data, shared mutable state bugs
Use for: large datasets, CPU-bound operations, independent elements
